author: Paweł Huryn
text: Claude Code already shipped a solution for this: hooks. PreToolUse runs before any tool executes. Your script sees the tool name + arguments and returns allow, block, or error. Block rm. Allow edits. Require confirmation for writes to /src. Log every Bash command.
recencyNote: Status ID 2033663104773390679 — estimated April 1-3, 2026. Individual product manager / PM educator (The Product Compass, 26.2K followers verified). Not in R1-R5 (R4 captured his Amazon/Kiro post at a different status ID).
topicRelevance: AI agent harness and security — Claude Code hooks implement exactly the pre-tool enforcement layer that is missing from most agentic deployments. The ability to block, allow, or error on any tool call before execution is the harness primitive that enterprise security teams need. Directly relevant to Deep Agents' harness engineering thesis and its intersection with enterprise AI security.
suggestedEngagement: The PreToolUse hook pattern is the harness-layer enforcement primitive that most enterprise teams are missing — they're thinking about access control at the model level (prompts and guardrails) rather than at the tool execution boundary. Asking: has he found any patterns for making hook decisions context-aware (e.g., block 'rm' in /src but allow it in /tmp based on workflow state)?

The 'log every Bash command' point is undervalued — for regulated enterprises, a complete audit trail of every tool invocation is a compliance requirement, not just a debug aid. This turns Claude Code into an auditable agent executor. Ask whether he's seen anyone wiring these logs into a SIEM or enterprise audit pipeline yet.

The PreToolUse → PostToolUse hook pair is even more powerful: pre-enforce policy, post-validate outcomes. Together they make agentic execution verifiable step-by-step. Ask whether he's experimented with hooks that escalate to human review for high-blast-radius tool calls (e.g., production DB writes) rather than blocking outright.

author: Adam Rackis
text: Something nobody's talking about: Senior engineers have to review AI code. Cool. But how do junior and mid-levels become senior without years of writing code by hand? Smashing the magic button and tossing the result to a senior engineer for review does not make you a senior engineer.

topicRelevance: Software engineering productivity — bold take on the second-order effect of AI coding tools on the engineering talent pipeline. As AI-assisted code raises the productivity ceiling for senior engineers, it simultaneously compresses the learning path that makes engineers senior in the first place. Directly relevant to the enterprise engineering productivity discussion and to Deep Agents' positioning around the 'orchestrators not writers' thesis.
suggestedEngagement: The compounding problem is that the same orgs mandating AI adoption for productivity are also the ones with the thinnest senior review bench — Amazon's 1,500-engineer AI mandate led to Sev-1 outages partly because the review layer wasn't scaled with the code generation velocity. Ask whether he thinks the fix is process (more mandatory review gates) or tooling (AI-assisted review that flags when AI-generated code is being AI-reviewed).

text: How Amazon's AI coding tool deleted a Production environment. Recently, AWS engineers gave their agentic coding tool, Kiro, a simple task: fix a small issue in Cost Explorer. topicRelevance: AI agent security in enterprise — the Kiro production deletion incident is the canonical 2026 case study for agentic AI blast radius risk. suggestedEngagement: The Kiro incident is a perfect illustration of the 'task scope vs. action scope' problem in agentic deployments — the agent was given a narrow task but had unrestricted action scope. The 13-hour outage is the blast radius quantified — it's not a theoretical risk. Ask whether he thinks process controls scale to the volume of AI-assisted changes Amazon is generating, or whether automation of the review layer is necessary.

The pattern (mandate adoption, suppress dissent, hit incident) is a governance failure before it's a technical one.
